knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

## Why this example matters

The `sleepstudy` design is balanced and dense. Beat the Blues provides the
contrasting case: 100 randomized participants were scheduled at months
0, 2, 3, 5, and 8, but the retained public teaching fixture contains 380
observations because of attrition. Three participants have only one retained
observation and therefore no direct slope information.

This contrast demonstrates how the diagnostic behaves; it is not evidence
that one schedule type is always superior.

## Load the frozen teaching fixture

```{r data}
library(lme4)
library(slopeaudit)

path <- system.file("extdata", "btheb_primary.csv", package = "slopeaudit")
btheb <- read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

btheb$subject <- factor(btheb$subject)
btheb$occasion <- factor(
  btheb$occasion,
  levels = c("0", "2", "3", "5", "8")
)
btheb$treatment <- factor(btheb$treatment, levels = c("TAU", "BtheB"))

c(participants = nlevels(btheb$subject), observations = nrow(btheb))
```

`month_c = month - 4` centers the model's time basis at Month 4. The target
remains a linear change in BDI score per month over Months 0--8.

```{r models}
control <- lmerControl(
  optimizer = "nloptwrap",
  optCtrl = list(maxeval = 200000),
  check.conv.singular = "message"
)

full <- lmer(
  bdi ~ treatment * occasion + (1 + month_c | subject),
  data = btheb,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = control
)

null <- lmer(
  bdi ~ treatment * occasion + (1 | subject),
  data = btheb,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = control
)

month_target <- list(
  basis_type = "linear",
  outcome_units = "BDI score points",
  time_or_exposure_scale = "1 month",
  origin_or_reference = "Month 4 (month_c = 0)",
  reference_window = "Months 0--8",
  estimand = "participant-specific linear change in BDI score per month"
)
```

## Decompose the fitted slope

```{r decomposition}
sources <- slope_decomposition(full, "month_c", month_target)
sources
```

The manuscript-frozen homogeneous-independent-residual reference has 100
participants, 380 observations, and these equal-participant means:

| Quantity | Mean |
|---|---:|
| `R_direct` | 0.19785 |
| `D_slope2` | 0.21487 |
| `Delta_fit` | 0.01703 |

The participant table records three `has_direct_slope_information = FALSE`
rows. Those participants can still receive fitted random-slope predictions
through the model, but their outcome schedules contain no direct within-person
slope contrast. That distinction is exactly why `D_slope2` must not be called
direct evidence of change.

## Run the heterogeneity test

```{r audit, eval=FALSE}
audit_999 <- slope_audit(
  full = full,
  null = null,
  target = "month_c",
  target_metadata = month_target,
  B = 999L,
  seed = 20260803L,
  progress = interactive()
)

audit_999
```

The observed likelihood-ratio statistic is about 4.072. In the frozen
manuscript workflow, the `B = 999` Monte Carlo interval crossed `.05`, so the
run was explicitly escalated. The `B = 4999` result was approximately `.074`
and Question 1 was **unsupported by these data**.

```{r escalate, eval=FALSE}
audit_4999 <- slope_audit(
  full = full,
  null = null,
  target = "month_c",
  target_metadata = month_target,
  B = 4999L,
  seed = 20260803L,
  progress = interactive()
)
```

The reader-facing conclusion is therefore **STOP—INDIVIDUAL-SLOPE CLAIM**.
The returned decomposition may still describe the fitted positive-variance
model, but only conditionally. Do not write “there is no slope heterogeneity,”
and do not use fitted individual slopes as though their population variation
had been established.

## Scope of this worked model

This example deliberately uses the manuscript's homogeneous independent
residual specification. It does not claim that `lme4` fitted AR(1),
occasion-specific residual variances, or a nonlinear time effect. Those are
separate model-sensitivity questions. A defensible correlated-residual model
fitted elsewhere may be represented by participant-specific `R` matrices in
the matrix design route, but it must not be mislabeled as an `lme4` fit.
